6. Syed Mokaddas Ali, learned Advocate, appearing for the opposite party-complainant, on the other hand, submits that sufficient ingredients of sections 406/420 of the Penal Code having been disclosed in the petition of complaint and there is sufficient material to support the complaint and the allegations made in the complaint, this case cannot be quashed. In support of his submission, learned Advocate relied on a number of decisions. Learned Advocate relied on the case of Salahuddin (Md) vs State, reported in 51 DLR 299, the case of Nurul Islam vs State, reported in 49 DLR 464, the case of Shamsul Islam Chowdhury vs Uttara Bank Ltd, reported in 11 BLC 119, the case of Nasiruddin Mahmud vs Momtazuddin Ahmed, reported in 36 DLR (AD) 14, the case of Md Arifur Rahman vs Shantosh Kumar Sadhu, reported in 1994 BLD (AD) 78, the case of Munshi Md Rashed Kamal vs Abdus Salam, reported in 10 BLC (AD) 186, the case of Akamuddin Ahmed vs State, reported in 27 DLR (AD) 175, the Case of Amir Hossain vs MA Malek, reported in 56 DLR (AD) 146, the case of Sarwar M Kamal vs State, reported in 9 BLC 436 and the case of Hajee Khabiruddin Ahmed vs Md Salam Kabir, reported in 34 DLR (AD) 271. 

 9. A case can be quashed only on prosecution or complainant's materials and on admitted facts. If a complaint does not disclose the ingredients of section under which it has been made, then the proceeding can be quashed. In the decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 28 it has been settled that a proceeding can be quashed even before exhausting the provisions of law when the fact is preposterous or if it appears from reading of the complaint that it does not disclose any cause of action or if the petition of complaint resembles certain other nature of case that is, if it disclose a civil nature then it can be quashed. 

 15. The decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the complainant opposite party i.e. the case of HMM Alam vs Bangladesh, reported in 9 BLC 331 is relating to Artha Rin Adalat Ain, the case of Amir Hossain vs MA Malek reported in 56 DLR (AD) 146 where it has been held that there is no bar for the complainant to proceed side by side with the winding up proceeding of the company owned by the complainant-petitioner and the convict-respondent, the case of Akamuddin Ahmed vs State, reported in 27 DLR (AD)175 it has been held that a dishonest concealment of facts is a deception within the meaning of section 415 of the Penal Code, the case of Munshi Md Rashed Kamal vs Abdus Salam reported in 10 BLC (AD) 186 is a case under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and it has been held that a cheque can be presented to the bank within six months but the notice must be sent within 15 days of the receipt of the information from the bank, the case of Md Arifur Rahman vs Shantosh Kumar Sadhu reported in 1994 BLD (AD) 78 where it has been held that to establish a case under section 415 of the Penal Code it is a settled principle that the initial intention to deceive must be established, the case of Nasiruddin Mahmud vs Momtazuddin Ahmed reported in 36 DLR (AD) 14 where the same principle as under section 415 of the Penal Code was propounded, the case of Nurul Islam vs State, reported in 49 DLR 464 and the case of Salahuddin vs State, reported in 51 DLR 299 it has been held that section 265C provides for an alternative remedy but it cannot take away the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and lastly, the decision of Shamsul Islam Chowdhury (Md) vs Uttara Bank Ltd, reported in 11 BLC 119 settled when a cause of action of a case under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act arose. Learned Advocate fully relied on the decision reported in 9 BLC where the question posted before their Lordships was, that the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing to the drawer of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, the date for receiving the notice is to be mentioned in the complaint. All these decisions, on the facts of the instant case, are not applicable as we find in the instant case there was a business transaction and an agreement was arrived at between the parties where some clauses for fulfilment of the agreement were agreed by the parties. Here the decision reported in 2005 BLD 321 is applicable as in the similar condition and the case was under sections 406/420 of the Penal Code, their Lordships quashed the proceeding on the ground that there was a business transaction between the parties. This decision also finds support from the decision reported in 1987 BLD 133 and 51 DLR (AD) 280 where it has been held that for breach of contract relating to business transaction, the dispute is to be sorted out in the civil Court. In the instant case it is an admitted fact that the parties after entering into an agreement, the complainant delivered the medical equipment whereupon, as per agreement, accused petitioner issued cheques, the agreement made room for realisation of money and when same has not been paid in terms of the agreement, we are of the view that the facts of the instant case disclose a civil liability. We find substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.
